extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers of Montaigne / readers interested in moral philosophy and essays
extracted.subtask_description: A Renaissance personal essay exploring attitudes toward death, the effects of imagination on body and behavior, and practical/psychological counsel for living and sexual performance. The text mixes anecdotes, classical quotations, and reflections rather than giving formal rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premeditation of death is a great advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: “to premeditate is doubtless a very great advantage” — thinking about death beforehand reduces its terror and prepares one for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that premeditation can lessen disturbance when the time comes; Nature assists (sudden violent death leaves no leisure for fear; slow illness leads to a natural loathing of life and diminished terror). He notes he finds it harder to resolve on death when healthy than when languishing of a fever. Example: Caesar’s remark to a decrepit soldier. Implication: mentally rehearsing or making death familiar confers real psychological benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity with gradual decline reduces shock
rubrics_metrics.description: “Nature, leading us by the hand, an easy and, as it were, an insensible pace, step by step conducts us to that miserable state, and by that means makes it familiar to us.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne contrasts sudden loss (which humanity could not endure) with the insensible pace of aging; because decline is gradual we become insensitive to the stroke. Thus observing ordinary changes and declines helps acclimate one to mortality and lessen panic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate a firm, undisturbed soul (sovereignty of the soul)
rubrics_metrics.description: The soul should be 'firm and erect' so it is not at rest while standing in fear; when mastered it becomes 'sovereign of all her lusts and passions, mistress of necessity, shame, poverty, and all the other injuries of fortune.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne uses classical quotations to recommend a temper of mind that is not shaken by tyrants, storms, or the 'strong hand of thundering Jove.' This inner steadiness is presented as true and sovereign liberty on earth and a defense against fear, violence, injustice, prisons, and chains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contempt of life and acceptance of death as rational/religious foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: “Our very religion itself has no surer human foundation than the contempt of life...the argument of reason invites us to it--for why should we fear to lose a thing, which being lost, cannot be lamented?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne claims reason and religion support contempt of life (or at least not fearing death). He appeals to Socrates and Stoic ideas: fearing all possible deaths eternally is worse than undergoing the single inevitable one. Death is inevitable and thus not to be irrationally feared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of life depends on use of time, not length
rubrics_metrics.description: “The utility of living consists not in the length of days, but in the use of time; a man may have lived long, and yet lived but a little.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne advises making use of the present time; long life does not change the duration of death, and comparing lives by length is foolish. Practical implication: aim to live well rather than merely long.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elaborate funerary/medical ceremonies magnify fear of death
rubrics_metrics.description: “I believe...that it is those terrible ceremonies and preparations wherewith we set it out, that more terrify us than the thing itself...a dark room, set round with burning tapers; our beds environed with physicians and divines...nothing but ghostliness and horror round about us.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that the outward trappings and theatrical preparations (wailing, rituals, doctors' attendance, dark rooms) increase terror; a death that leaves no leisure for such ceremonials is happier. Implication: removing melodramatic trappings makes death less frightening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination has real, often harmful physical power
rubrics_metrics.description: “I am one of those who are most sensible of the power of imagination: every one is jostled by it, but some are overthrown by it...The very sight of another’s pain materially pains me, and I often usurp the sensations of another person.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne gives many examples (coughs transmitted, fevers born of fancy, people dying at the sight of the hangman, horns growing in dreams becoming real) to show imagination can produce bodily effects, illnesses, and even death. Practical counsel: recognize imagination’s capacity to make or worsen symptoms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exposure to others' suffering when emotionally close
rubrics_metrics.description: “I more unwillingly visit the sick in whom by love and duty I am interested, than those I care not for...I take possession of the disease I am concerned at, and take it to myself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because empathy/imagination can 'usurp' another's disease, Montaigne recommends avoiding scenarios where one’s imagination will adopt another's suffering. He notes physicians may deliberately cultivate or guard against such contagion of imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre‑declaration/confession can mitigate imagination-driven failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne tells of a man whose recurring frigidity was cured when he frankly confessed his subjection beforehand; knowing it was expected eased his restraint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telling the partner or otherwise anticipating the problem reduces anxiety and the restraining power of imagination. In other words, social disclosure can serve as a psychological remedy against imagined or expected malfunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not force sexual performance; proceed gradually and practically
rubrics_metrics.description: “Married people...ought never to compel or so much as to offer at the feat, if they do not find themselves quite ready: and it is less unseemly to fail...and to await another opportunity at more private and more composed leisure, than to make himself perpetually miserable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne counsels gradual trials, light offers, and avoidance of obstinate attempts to 'force an absolute conquest' when subject to performance anxiety. Practical strategies noted: take trials little by little, come half-sated, use reassurance; aging may reduce the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some successful practical remedies against sexual failure
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: those who 'secure themselves' by coming half sated; others reassured by friends or counter-charms; age can lessen impotence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne lists concrete tactics that have helped men: tempering desire by partial satiety, gaining assurance from a friend (or counter-charm), and relying on the reduced ardour of age. These are pragmatic approaches rather than moralizing prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Many bodily functions act independently of the will — mitigate moral blame
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne emphasizes that parts of the body often refuse to perform at the precept of the will and perform without it: hairs stand on end, hands reach parts involuntarily, the tongue is frozen, vessels dilate without consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In defending those blamed for involuntary failures (e.g., sexual failure), recognize the physiological independence of organs; culpability should be tempered by understanding involuntary bodily action. He even provocatively argues in defense of the member, noting the universal mutinies of bodily parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physicians and healers exploit imagination (placebo and suggestion)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Why do the physicians possess, before hand, their patients’ credulity with so many false promises of cure, if not to the end, that the effect of imagination may supply the imposture of their decoctions?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne notes physicians knowingly harness patients' credulity and imagination to produce cures; the sight of medicine alone can work on some. Practical implication: understand the therapeutic role of suggestion and the limits of physical remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid subtle counterfeit or trick actions despite occasional efficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne admits to using a trick (the medal/ribbon) to alleviate a bridegroom’s fear but says he is 'an enemy to all subtle and counterfeit actions, and abominate all manner of trickery, though it be for sport, and to an advantage; for though the action may not be vicious in itself, its mode is vicious.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a ruse can exploit fancy and succeed (because 'our fancy being so far seduced'), the author warns about the moral mode of such trickery. The guidance is to prefer honest remedies and to be wary of deceptive means even when they work.
